CausalChain: TME stresses (hypoxia, cytokines) -> Pharmacologic modulation via nanocarrier delivery and localized imaging -> Transient disruption of tight junction integrity -> Increased surface exposure of Claudin18.2 epitopes -> Enhanced binding/internalization of claudin18.2-targeted agents (ADC, bispecific antibodies, CAR-T cells) -> Synergistic antitumor activity with microenvironment modulation
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that the application of a transient, localized pharmacologic modulation strategy—using nanocarriers loaded with tight junction-disrupting agents and guided by real-time imaging—to the tumor microenvironment will safely and reversibly disrupt tight junction integrity. This deliberate modulation will increase the surface exposure of Claudin18.2 epitopes on tumor cells. Consequently, the subsequent administration of Claudin18.2-targeted therapies (including ADCs, bispecific antibodies, and CAR-T cells) will experience enhanced binding and internalization, leading to improved antitumor responses. This approach builds upon the natural tendency of TME stresses to alter tight junction organization by adding a controlled, technology-enhanced step that optimizes treatment efficacy.
Abstract: This study proposes a novel, technology-enabled approach to improve the efficacy of Claudin18.2-targeted therapies in Claudin18.2-positive cancers. We hypothesize that the use of transient, localized pharmacologic modulation of the tumor microenvironment (TME), facilitated by nanocarrier-mediated delivery systems and real-time imaging, can safely and reversibly disrupt tight junction integrity. This disruption transiently increases the surface exposure of Claudin18.2 epitopes, thereby enhancing the binding, internalization, and cytotoxic action of targeted therapies such as antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), bispecific antibodies, and CAR-T cells. By integrating advanced drug delivery platforms and imaging modalities, our approach not only leverages the intrinsic TME stresses (e.g., hypoxia, cytokines) that naturally alter tight junction organization but also provides a controlled method to maximize therapeutic accessibility and efficacy without compromising tissue integrity.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that transient pharmacologic modulation of the TME would increase Claudin18.2 exposure to enhance targeted therapy efficacy. In our refined hypothesis, we retain the core idea of inducing transient disruption of tight junctions; however, we introduce a targeted, technology-based approach using nanocarriers and real-time imaging to achieve localized and reversible modulation. This enhancement directly addresses concerns regarding specificity, safety, and the controlled nature of tight junction disruption. While the original causal chain relied solely on endogenous TME stresses, the new hypothesis supplements this by strategically leveraging modern drug delivery and imaging technologies to precisely time and localize the modulation, thereby reinforcing each step of the causal chain.
